Q: How to load env vars from .env before running C# tests through VS Code A:

This is not a 1:1 answer for the specific question, instead it is a general answer for those who land on this question seeking something similar like: "How to load env vars before running C# tests". It works whether running tests in GH tests or whether running tests locally. It is DRY and it handles the problem without worrying about building a specific .runsettings file or something else.

This adds an Environment variable for a single test, all unit tests, or a group of unit tests.

Note: LaunchSettings is not loaded, so this is a good way to setup tests to skip say a call to Azure KV during setup when tests are running.

namespace MyProject.Tests.Setup
{
[TestClass]
public class GlobalTestInitialization
{
[AssemblyInitialize]
public static void AssemblyInit(TestContext context)
{
// Set environment variables or perform other global setup here
Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable("DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT", "Development");
}
}
}

Q: Is there a well-defined difference between "normalizing" and "canonicalizing" data? A:

"Canonicalize" & "normalize" (from "canonical form" & "normal form") are two related general mathematical terms that also have particular uses in particular contexts per some exact meaning given there. It is reasonable to label a particular process by one of those terms when the general meaning applies.

Your characterizations of those specific uses are fuzzy. The formal meanings for general & particular cases are more useful.

Sometimes given a bunch of things we partition them (all) into (disjoint) groups--"equivalence classes"--of ones that we consider to be in some particular sense similar or the same--"equivalent". The members of a group/class are the same/equivalent according to some particular condition--its equivalence relation.

We pick a particular member as the representative thing from each group/class & call it the canonical form for that group & its members. Two things are equivalent exactly when they are in the same equivalence class. Two things are equivalent exactly when their canonical forms are equal.

A normal form might be a canonical form or just one of several distinguished members.

To canonicalize/normalize is to find or use a canonical/normal form of a thing.

Wikipedia:

The distinction between "canonical" and "normal" forms varies by subfield. In most fields, a canonical form specifies a unique representation for every object, while a normal form simply specifies its form, without the requirement of uniqueness.

Applying the definitions to your example: Have you a bunch of values that you are partitioning & are you picking some member(s) per each class instead of the other members of that class? Well you have JSON values and short of re-modeling them you are partitioning them per what same-class member they map to under a function. So you can reasonably call the result JSON values canonical forms of the inputs. If you characterize re-modeling as applicable to all inputs then you can also reasonably call the post-re-modeling form of those canonical values canonical forms of re-modeled input values. But if not then people probably won't complain that you call the re-modeled values canonical forms of the input values even though technically they wouldn't be.

Q: FILTER, ISNUMBER, SEARCH and FORMULATEXT returning #VALUE A:

For anyone else trying the same thing, it is the second array that was the problem, as I knew. I just didn't understand why. Well, I only needed to check for the formulas in the first column! The formulas are all the same, so that will get all the rows that I want filtered.

So, this for my sample data above, without my formula for figuring out the last column, works:

=FILTER($A$1:$K$12,ISNUMBER(SEARCH("=IF\*",FORMULATEXT($C$1:$C$12))))

And with finding my last column...

=FILTER($A$1:INDEX($1:1,COUNTIF($1:$1,"\>0"),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("=IF\*",FORMULATEXT($C$1:$C$12))))
